Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

mental adjective

of the mind

also mentally, mental health, mental illness, physically and mentally, psychological

classical

Cic. Fam. 7.1.1: et sine dolōre corporis tē fuisse et animō valuisse
Cic. Fin. 1.59 (Lewis & Short): animī morbī sunt cupiditātēs immēnsae et inānēs

animī

the genitive of animus, beside the noun it describes, often set against corporis

of the mind, mental

Classical Latin has no adjective for “mental”: it says “of the mind”, animī (animī dolor, mental pain; animī morbus, mental illness, in Cicero a vice or passion), or uses the ablative animō for “mentally” (animō valēre), against corpore, physically.

Other words

  • mentis — of the mind (as thinking, reason)

    the genitive of mēns · also used · classical

    Where the reason is meant rather than feeling: mentis compos, in one’s right mind (Traupman 155, compos mentis).

  • mentālis, mentāle — mental

    avoid · late Latin

    Found only once, in a late sermon falsely ascribed to Augustine (Lewis & Short); the classical way is the genitive animī or mentis.

Examples

  • utrumque laetor, et sine dolōre corporis tē fuisse et animō valuisse

    I’m glad of both: that you were free of bodily pain, and that you were mentally soundCic. Fam. 7.1.1

  • animī valentēs morbō tentārī nōn possunt, corpora possunt

    healthy minds cannot be attacked by disease; bodies canCic. Tusc. 4.31 (Lewis & Short)

See also arithmetic, emotion, attitude, health.

SourcesLewis & Short: animus · Lewis & Short: mens · Lewis & Short: mentalis · Lewis & Short: morbus
